speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the apportioning of quotas for carps, commonly known as goldfish, is prohibited; that the government ought to protect the spawning of goldfish which really need another generation to regenerate; that the fishing season in the Gulf of St. Lawrence opens only in late April and that fishermen in Gaspesia, Magdalen Islands and northern New Brunswick are now facing serious problems because big trawlers from coastal ports on the Gulf of St. Lawrence are plundering the sea bottoms of the gulf, particularly the Banc des Orphelins, which results in reducing the catch of deep sea fish, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That the government allow the Department of the Environment to take any concrete measure it would deem necessary to ensure fishermen in Gaspesia, Magdalen Islands and northern New Brunswick better catches in keeping with their needs and to forbid all trawlers which are not based within the limits of the gulf waters to fish in that area.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON SLAUGHTER OF CATTLE FOR BLUE TONGUE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas the Department of Agriculture has no real and concrete evidence that the eradication program for blue tongue disease through the slaughter of cattle in the south central area of British Columbia will be successful because the disease is known to be spread by flies which can easily fly across the Canadian-U.S. border, because deer and other wildlife animals are known to be carriers of this disease, and because there is ample evidence that this disease has been in the area for years, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco):
That the Department of Agriculture establish a moratorium on this slaughter program until the full extent of this disease can be checked throughout Canada.

speechtext: To what extent is linguistic knowledge of (a) English, (b) French a factor in promotions to and within the commissioned officer class in the Canadian Army?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: BILINGUALISM-KNOWLEDGE OF ENGLISH AND FRENCH AS FACTORS FOR PROMOTION
speechtext:
(a) and (b) Linguistic knowledge of both English and French is not a factor in promotions to commissioned rank and within commissioned ranks up to the rank of Captain. However, in all officer classifications, (except for some specialist officer's classifications) knowledge of English is necessary to complete classification training which is a prerequisite to promotion within commissioned ranks up to the rank of Captain. For promotion to the rank of Major and above linguistic ability in a second official language is a factor. The total scoring system which determines relative merit is based on two major appraisal scores, "Performance and Potential". "Performance" accounts for 80 per cent and "Potential" for 20 per cent of the total possible merit score, and linguistic ability is one of the factors considered under "Potential". Other factors under "Potential" are qualifications, experience, personality, age and such other factors considered appropriate by the promotion board membership. Thus linguistic ability in a second official language, whether English or French should enhance an officer's position with respect to promotion to the ranks of Major or above in relation to a unilingual contemporary when all other factors are equal.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, April 27, consideration of Bill C-89, to amend the Anti-Inflation Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in my place at this time. Having spoken last night for five minutes, I did not appreciate that today I would be honoured by the return of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp). From the grassroots of the House of Commons, not just through the House leaders, I should like to congratulate him and to echo and repeat ad infinitum the good wishes that we all have for him regarding the very happy step he took at Easter. I would not pontificate about the Easter message, but I would question the fact that the government House leader took only a week's Easter recess. In view of what happened over the Easter recess to the President of the Privy Council, I think he would have had the almost unanimous blessing of members on all sides of the House if he had taken two, three, or perhaps even four weeks to make sure that the happy union that occurred at Easter shall continue thereafter, as I am sure it will.
After those Goldilocks words and, as the leader of the Social Credit party said, after the happy moonglow of romance, I find it difficult now to shift from platitutes about honeymoons and marriage to the realities of the Anti-Inflation Board. Not since the doctor created Frankenstein has there been a creation on the floor of this House to equal Bill C-89. There are many of us humble people from the grassroots of Canada who believe in what our leader has said. We campaigned, we fought, we talked, and sometimes we were even questioned about what went on in that grand old election campaign of July, 1974. I was one of those who took a stand in trying to defend something that was vital to Canada, with all its imperfections.
Like other members in my party, I took a stand and our party was politically lacerated by the people of Canada: we are not now sitting over there. I will not waste too much time on sad, bittersweet memories or thoughts of what might have been-because we will be there. One thing that many people can say about the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), my former leader, is that he may have many pluses and he may have many minuses, but he speaks because he believes in something, and because he believes, he remains true. He did not do a flip-flop like this government. This government is like a gosh darn cookie jar in a lumberjack camp. This government wanted to cook pancakes; they put all the ingredients into the old frying pan.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: Come to the point.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Now we hear from the mountain member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane). If he wants to
Anti-Inflation Act
get involved in this debate, I would like him to speak now or go back to his riding and try to match his words of today with what he said in July, 1974. There may be a Gregorian calendar, a Christian calendar and there may be a Judaic-Christian calendar. The fact of the matter is that my happy friend from Hamilton Mountain, who is one of the lovelier people in this House, cannot face himself in the mirror. That is why the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) does not shave his face; that is why he has a beard.
I am amazed that the hon. member from "Happy Mountain", or the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain, has the temerity to even look in the mirror. I guess he does shave, though, and has never got over the baby fuzz. "Happy Gus MacFarlane, I do not know how you can face yourself in the mirror after the way you people campaigned in July, 1974, as compared to the facts of reality today." In any event, I do not want to get too political.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: Go ahead, Pat.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
I do not want to get too political, but the fact of the matter is, in very serious vein, that my colleague the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) has moved an amendment to a clause that in fact will allow controls for 18 months. Then my happy friend the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), who has to find happiness somewhere, and my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who is a happy fellow too, have concocted what I call the maypole dance. They have proposed a subamendment, not to have controls for 18 months but to end them on May 1, 1976. I am not going to waste too much time trying to analyse that subamendment because, quite frankly, it has no credence at all when taken in the light of what this party believes in or what this party stood for and campaigned for, namely, that this government should get off its duff and try to do something about inflation. This subamendment comes from my friends to the left, and they are so far to the left that I think they should be locked up in some type of sanatorium. They are so far to the left that obviously they do not put any credence in the fight that every Canadian is trying to win that is, the fight against inflation.
I said last night, in the few remarks I made before the hour of ten o'clock, that I respected the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and Jean-Luc Pepin, chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, and that I had some respect for the government. However, unless each individual Canadian begins to fins some personal solution to inflation, quite frankly we are not going to dampen these inflationary fires. The point is that some hon. members in the back row across the way have lately echoed what my leader has said. We want a 90-day freeze to wet the towels of all Canadians across the country so that we can get out of this inflationary psychology. We want people to stop and think before buying, perhaps because they know the cost will be 20 per cent lower tomorrow. This might cause people to pause and think. Perhaps that is what this government should do: it should begin to think.
Coming back to the bill-and I am very serious about this-this is the party that wanted some type of government intervention, and this was part of our campaing back in July, 1974. I found it very difficult to campaign because-

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: Order, please. Before returning the floor to the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) I should indicate that his remaining time is rather short.

speechtext: How many minutes?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
I am not going to take up those three minutes in answering the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). I am talking about integrity, and the fact of the matter is, as I said last night, if you are really going to sell the inflation package, the person who should sell it is the leader of the land, your Prime Minister and my Prime Minister. Why is that right hon. gentleman, who is a persuasive man, not out across this country from sea to sea preaching the message of belt-tightening, discipline and integrity? The reason he is not, has not and will not, is that there is no integrity: he has done a flip-flop that is the biggest pancake in the political history of Canada.

Getting back to the anti-inflation bill, this country of Canada in 1968 was caught up in something called "Trudeaumania". Many members won and are here. There were many members on this side who lost as a result of that so-called "Trudeaumania". It is a sad thing to this particular member of parliament, who happened to win in spite of Trudeaumania, that the so-called just society will, under Bill C-89, become a controlled society. I am seriously suggesting to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all my colleagues in this House that controls are alien to the Canadian public. This country was not built on controls. It was built on the initiative of individuals who were sometimes rewarded by tax incentives.
One of the reasons I do not hesitate to support the amendment of the hon. member for York-Simcoe, who is trying to restrict the controls to a period of 18 months, is that this bill is not designed to allow controls for three years but allows, by order in council, the Treasury Board to impose controls ad infinitum. Controls are alien to the North American continent, and certainly to parliament. This bill distorts the economic picture. I give great credit to my friends to the left for their sincerity and because some of them are school teachers. I have a brother-in-law in Nova Scotia who is a school teacher. The package in respect of the school teachers in Nova Scotia which was brought before the Anti-inflation Board has been distorted. These teachers did not ask for an increase for a long period. However, through a collective agency which bargains for all teachers in Nova Scotia, a package was prepared which has been challenged by the Anti-Inflation Board.
We have the idiotic situation that the teachers in that province must come to Ottawa to make sure that they get what they are entitled to. Because they did not make a demand for three years, what they have asked for in a one-year period appears to be above the guidelines set out by this government. They are being penalized by school boards in other parts of this country who have successfully negotiated in the last three years and are far above the level of the teachers in Nova Scotia. They are so far behind they can never catch up. There is no more responsible body in Nova Scotia than these teachers.
This is one reason controls are anathema to this country. I would not be in the House of Commons if there was equality. I am here because of the fundamental disparities and differences which are our curse and our challenge. That is why this House of Commons must deal in its funny way with procedural rules which are almost archaic and which you, Mr. Speaker, labour on and on to give fundamental judgments. However, you are a captive of this system that has been a fundamental part of our procedure.
In any class in which I have spoken to my students I always told them that when this House of Commons is in session it is the closest thing there is to the heart of Canada. I do not know of another institution which is so symbolically representative of the 23 million or 24 million Canadians, even with all its imperfections. Earlier I said that I would not be here if we had controls, because if we had controls and equality in my area we would never have survived.
April 28, 1976

I think, quite frankly, that the strength of this country lies in what the late right hon. member for Algoma East, Lester B. Pearson, used to say. He said that through diversity there is strength, and with unity there is common cause. Here we have a long-term control package at a time when we have escalating energy problems in Atlantic Canada, where people on moderate incomes have electricity bills of $300 and $400.
The fabric of this country is not based on linguistics or on race. This is an integral part of the country, but we must do something about an economic condition. As yet there has not been too much hue and cry from the people of Atlantic Canada. This is the reason I am happy to have an opportunity to participate in this debate on the amendment. We go along with controls that are down to earth, but I will never vote for a bill that puts controls in force for three years which, by order in council, can be extended ad infinitum. I am amazed that the Minister of Finance could acquiesce in this. I am amazed that he would ask the opposition to become an accessory before the fact in respect of Bill C-89.
The cabinet will change, and we do not know what attitude another cabinet will have. Ministers come and go. Very many of them will go. In fact, they should all go and I hope they do. Seriously, however, I cannot understand how my good friend from Rosedale, the Minister of Finance, who has taken constitutional law, let alone any government whether Liberal, Conservative or, in the name of infamy, NDP, could have brought in an open-ended program of controls. While I was interested in the endorsation of the just society, I will not be a part of this controlled society.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has returned. I am always interested in noting the behaviour of the Minister of Finance. He seems either to take some words out of context to take simplistic attitudes or come to simplistic conclusions concerning the attitude of the opposition. Yesterday he referred to the remarks of my colleague for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). He referred to what he claimed might have been insincere words and attitudes by the former leader of our party the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), with regard to parts of this bill.
Bill C-89 is not only concerned with the granting of the right of appeal from decisions of the Anti-Inflation Board by salaried and hourly-rated workers or parties to a decision, but there is something much more fundamental. There is an amending of section 46 of Bill C-73, which has to do with the period of these controls and the procedures and formulas that may be adopted. I think it was dishonest of the minister to say what he did about this party. This party voted in favour of Bill C-73 on second reading in order to have it sent to the committee, although we had reservations which were clearly expressed by the then leader of the party and other spokesmen in respect of the period of controls which we considered to be excessive.
We said we would do everything we could to have the period shortened and, depending on the action and attitude of the government in committee, we would then reserve our position at third reading. We voted against the bill at third reading, as we had undertaken, because the govern-
Anti-Inflation Act
ment refused to change it one iota except for the introduction of a review formula that was of little consequence. In the same way, there is nothing insincere about our having voted for Bill C-89 to go to the committee. That is not approval of the bill. This is the reason I say it is wrong for the Minister of Finance simply to say we voted before for this bill on second reading, and now are bitterly complaining about it and doing a flip-flop. That is not so. It was clearly indicated that we wanted to see the bill go forward to committee. That is where bills are supposed to be studied. The Minister of Finance is the author of the present rules under which we operate. All he has to do is review the speeches he made in proposing and supporting the rules.
My colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), in committee raised a point with regard to the power of the governor in council to extend by way of order in council the ambit of the Anti-Inflation Board under Bill C-73. Even with regard to the construction industry section 3(2)(b)(i) provides for a limitation of jurisdiction on firms employing 20 or more persons. Yet we now see the jurisdiction extended to all construction firms, even one-man firms. I wish hon. members and other persons outside the House, particularly those who write and comment about what goes on in the House, would realise that under section 12 of Bill C-73 the governor in council has the right to refer a question of extension to the AntiInflation Board, the board then will consider it and make a recommendation back to the governor in council, who in turn issues an order in council implementing the recommendation of the AIB as to the extension of jurisdiction.
It is as simple as taking a tennis ball, bouncing it against a wall and then having it come back to the hand, because the governor in council is extending the jurisdiction of controls not only from the few Galbraithian, selective controls that they allege were to be have been the basis of this program last October, and then in November and December, but from when the legislation was under consideration in the House. How is it to be done? Not straightforward, but covertly, as I have said, by throwing a ball against the wall and catching it. The government say it thinks it would like to extend the jurisdiction of controls over this or that section of the economy. They turn to the Anti-Inflation Board, which merely reflects back the thinking in the form of a recommendation, and on that recommendation which was generated by the governor in council the order in council is issued and the extension made. Wage increases of 20 per cent or more for 15,000 public servants, most of them employees of Ontario school boards.

The motion put forward by my hon. friend from York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) attempts at least to apply some measure of reality with respect to the continuance of a program whose benefits, whatever they might be, cannot be expected to continue for an indefinite period. As a number of speakers have well stated, we face a major difficulty here. It is one thing for the minister to introduce a program which will last for up to three years. It is quite another for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to indicate subsequently, along with the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, that the program of controls is not really a short-term program-if one can refer to three years as being a short period-but that it might be prolonged to become a more comprehensive system of economic controls than anything we have so far experienced.
All members realize that an economy such as ours is not one which operates on an eighteenth century or nineteenth century laissez-faire model. On the other hand, if the government is planning to change substantially the rules under which a mixed economy such as ours operates, then surely it should not do so unilaterally and, in particular, it ought not to do so on the pretext of dealing with one particular phenomenon, namely, inflation. That is the difficulty we face under the present program and its continuance for three years.
Economists not only in our own country but in countries which have had a good deal of experience in the operation of anti-inflation programs concede that such programs are indeed useful during periods in which the fires of inflation appear to be out of control, in periods when great damage is done, particularly to those living on low or fixed incomes. But it has also been concluded by a number of these economic experts that controls exercised for too long a period not only destroy the traditional economic pattern but are extremely harmful to the very people they are supposed to benefit.
This brings me back once again to the people I represent, to those who have to live in areas of great regional disparity, far from the centres of the decision-making goes on with respect to economic policy, people who far too often become the victims of the heavily centralist approach which is so involved in programs of the kind we are considering today. To my mind, the remarks of Jean-Luc Pepin and the remarks made by the Prime Minister have been in no way helpful to the credibility of the scheme for which the Minister of Finance is directly responsible. It must have been chilling for members to read the statement of the Canadian Labour Congress in the annual report and recommendations made to the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet. What disturbed me was not only the rhetoric contained in that document and the extent to which a significant section of the economy so totally rejected the government's program, but the degree to which neither side appeared able to engage in a useful conversation with the other.
We live in a time of very large institutions. We in this chamber do not have to ask ourselves how large the institution of government has become. We are well aware of it. We are also well aware of the strength of the big corporations. One of the other major segments of our society is organized labour. It is not as large here as it is in Britain or in certain other European countries, but it is certainly a

significant factor. From the outset, the Minister of Finance has not been able to produce any objective argument in support of his contention that three years is the correct period, the period necessary if the program is to achieve whatever virtues it is expected to produce. The motion which has been placed before us deals realistically with a predicament which must surely have occurred to members on the government side. What I am saying is that, particularly with respect to Atlantic Canada, the longer the anti-inflation program continues the less likelihood we have of getting away from the kind of centralized decisions which have not been helpful in the past. It is obvious that a program which looks at things, presumably, from a national perspective but becomes greatly coloured by the influence of the central regions is slow to take into account particular problems in Atlantic Canada or in the Atlantic portion of Quebec or in western Canada.
I trust hon. members will reflect on this aspect because there has not been a great deal of discussion so far on the impact of anti-inflation policy on regional development. I have attempted during the last few months to put questions to various ministers with respect to this matter. I believe it is incumbent, particularly upon the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, not simply to make recommendations in the secrecy of cabinet but to state publicly from time to time his views as to the real impact of the anti-inflation program on the effective reduction of regional disparity. This is necessary if the minister's own credibility and the credibility of his department are to be maintained. In the absence of such an assurance we shall find it most difficult in the future to defend any commitment made by the present government or any other with respect to making the reduction of regional economic and social discrepancies a cornerstone of the federal position.

In November of 1975 the CBC conducted a poll which showed that 61 per cent of the people supported the idea of wage and price controls. Six months later the proportion which supported controls had dropped to 53 per cent. To another question as to whether the people believed controls were being applied fairly or not, two thirds of the people polled indicated that they did not believe the government's control program was being conducted fairly for all people.

Who is actually opposing the government's wage and price controls, not just in speeches and in resolutions but by actually stopping work? It is not the blue-collar workers, the steelworkers, the autoworkers or the railway workers who have belonged to unions for 25 years or more. It is the teachers, the nurses, the policemen in New Brunswick, Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan. These groups, which a few years ago would have killed anybody who suggested that they belonged to the labour movement, have gone on strike and refused to accept the wage increases offered to them by their employers. They are saying in a graphic way that they are not going to accept the government's anti-inflation program.
The Minister of Finance should ask himself why it is that these white-collar workers, most of whom would consider themselves part of the middle class, are so militant. Why are they refusing-I am sure the minister would agree-to be good citizens? Why are they refusing to work despite the laws that this parliament has passed? They are refusing to work because their day to day experiences tell them that the anti-inflation program is nothing more nor less than a program to control wages and salaries. One has only to look at the fact that yesterday the Anti-Inflation Board approved an increase of one cent on a gallon of oil for two of the oil companies in the country. Similar approval was given a week or two ago to Imperial Oil.
Natural gas prices have gone up by about 30 per cent. If we can believe the policy statement tabled yesterday by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), the price will probably go up by 25 cents within the next couple of years, as will the price of oil. The cost of electric power has gone up. In Nova Scotia the price has virtually doubled within the last year. Municipal taxes in city after city are increasing by as much as 20 per cent. Housing costs are to go up, probably by another 10 per cent this year. The Anti-Inflation Board, which has been preening itself about how the cost of food has gone down, yesterday announced that food will increase in cost by 3 to 4 per cent in the next couple of months.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, is it any wonder that the ordinary people of this country are saying that the anti-inflation program is not working and that they are not going to support it? Even though we oppose the whole program and the way in which it is being administered, we did support the minister when finally, after a great deal of urging, having refused to face up to the unfairness of the situation, he brought in this bill permitting groups of workers who feel that a decision of the Anti-Inflation Board is unfair to them, to appeal. turned down the agreement and said that the company and the union would have to accept a reduction in wages. The minister is quoted in the Toronto Star as saying he agreed.
The INCO operation in Thompson employs about 2,800 workers. Last year International Nickel hired 3,100 workers. In other words, there was a turnover of more than 100 per cent. Who goes there and does not stay? I suggest it is single people who do not have any roots and probably live in company bunkhouses. If the Anti-Inflation Board decision is upheld, what will happen in the course of the next year is that the INCO operation will probably be short somewhere between 200 and 300 workers and the company will not be able to produce all the nickel possible which it could export at a good price. Hardly a week goes by when we do not read news stories and reports of discussions in the Ontario legislature about the dangers of working in the uranium mine at Elliot Lake and about the possibility of getting cancer being 200 or 300 per cent higher than in respect of workers anywhere else. Obviously, the workers at Elliot Lake and their union people think they should get some compensation for that danger. The company agreed partly because this was right and partly because of its knowledge that if it did not pay the same wages as those paid at Sault Ste. Marie or Sudbury they would not get the workers.
The Anti-Inflation Board has ordered that the wages be shaved. If that situation is allowed to exist and the wages in Elliot Lake are lower than at Sudbury or Sault Ste. There is no indication that the companies are not making a fair profit on their sales of copper in Canada. I have no objection to the companies charging every penny the international market will support for copper exported, but I do not think Canadian copper should be sold to the United States at less than U.S. copper, Chilean copper or Zambian copper. I see no reason why the Anti-Inflation Board should have permitted the two increases of almost 10 per cent in the price of copper in just over a month. I should like to appeal to the administrator to look at this. I hope he will be as tough in looking at that increase in price as he threatens to be in respect of increases in wages.
Because I have so little faith in the government's program I intend to support the subamendment put forward by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broad-bent) which calls for the ending of the program on May 1 of this year. Failing that, I will vote for the Conservative amendment.
